I’ve got about 8 mu of land here in Quzhou, and I’ve been working it for over thirty years now. I know every plot. Last October I sowed 6.5 mu of winter wheat—used Shixinmai 22, an improved variety that’s done well for me and the neighbors. The wheat is up and greening now, so my job this spring is to get it through to harvest in early June. I’ll irrigate three more times: once right now at green-up, once at jointing in May, and once during grain filling. For fertilizer, I put down compound at sowing last autumn, and I’ll topdress with urea at jointing. The extension fellow says 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but I’ve learned it’s safer to do about 18 kg N, 7.5 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium per mu—you lose more by going short than by going a little over. I’ll spray insecticide twice and herbicide once. If the weather cooperates, I expect around 1,000 jin per mu.

Right after wheat harvest in mid-June, I’ll plant summer maize on that same 6.5 mu. The turnaround is tight—sometimes only five or six days—so I won’t till. I’ll hire the no-till planter and sow Denghai 605 hybrid seed, about one package per mu. Maize gets less feed than wheat: roughly 14 kg nitrogen, 3 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. I’ll irrigate twice—once after sowing if it’s dry, and once at the big trumpet stage. Two or three pesticide sprays will handle the worms and weeds.

The other 1.5 mu I’m planting cotton in late April. Cotton gives me cash income in the fall when grain prices are still uncertain, and the price was decent last year. I’ll rotary till that lighter plot to warm the soil, then plant Guoxinmian improved seed. Cotton needs more attention—three irrigations and about five pesticide applications through the season. I expect about 550 jin of seed cotton per mu.

I thought about trying stevia like the big farm down the road, but my cousin tried it two years ago and the buyers were unreliable. Better to stick with what I know. Money is tight this year, but I’m not cutting back on fertilizer or irrigation—I’d rather borrow a little from family than risk a bad harvest.
